lead.headline: Nvidia's 14% Plunge Pushes Wall Street Into Correction as the AI Rout Goes Global
lead.dek: A reported SEC look at Nvidia’s accounting sent the S&P 500 down 3.6% for a seventh straight loss and the Nasdaq down 5%, after Taiwan, Korea and Japan fell 5%-6%; Treasuries rallied while gold and bitcoin were sold.
body: The S&P 500 has now fallen for seven straight sessions and closed Friday at 6,914.90, down 3.64% on the day and about 11.5% below its 6 October record, which puts it in correction alongside the Dow. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.01% to 22,682.49, erasing its gain for 2026, and the Philadelphia chip index fell 10.7%.

The trigger was a Reuters report that SEC enforcement staff are examining Nvidia's accounting. Nvidia fell 14% to $125.53 on roughly four times its normal volume, removing about $491bn of market value in a session; Reuters stressed that an inquiry is not evidence of wrongdoing. Anthropic, which listed at $83 on Thursday, slid 8.5% to $88.91, and AMD has lost about a fifth in two days after a short seller disclosed a position.

Asia had already broken before New York opened: Taiwan’s Taiex fell 6.23% to cap its worst week since 1991, the Kospi lost 5.21% and the Nikkei 5.06%. Germany’s DAX dropped 2.6% and 7.3% over the week. India was the exception, with the Sensex up 898 points to a nine-month high on record foreign buying.

Treasuries were the one haven that worked: the 10-year yield fell 12bp to 4.92% and the two-year 13bp to 4.63%, and the market trimmed the odds of a December Fed hike to about 90% from near-certainty in the morning. Gold, by contrast, sank to a 14-month low and bitcoin broke below $60,000, signs of forced selling across asset classes.

impact.title: What it means for markets
points: The AI hardware complex is now trading on accounting, policy and financing risk: Nvidia is down nearly 50% from its October high and the chip index lost 10.7% in a day, with Asian suppliers carrying the most beta.
With the VIX at 35.89 and an inverted volatility curve, the weekend leaves little room for error; Monday’s flash PMIs and Wednesday’s PCE come before a holiday-thinned Thanksgiving week.
Bonds have reasserted themselves as the hedge: a 12bp drop to 4.92% on the 10-year and a trimmed December hike probability (about 90%) are the first signs the rout is feeding into Fed pricing.
India stands out as a relative winner, with record foreign inflows of $12.21bn in November lifting the Nifty to a nine-month high, while Taiwan and Korea absorb the heaviest outflows.

read.title: The Ledger's Read
paragraphs: Friday turned a week of AI doubt into a full correction. The S&P 500's seventh straight fall took it more than 10% below its October record, and the trigger was not earnings but governance: a reported SEC look at Nvidia's accounting, on top of Jensen Huang's exit, a soft second day for Anthropic and a disclosed short in AMD. When the market's largest stock loses 14% in a session, index funds, volatility-targeting strategies and leveraged holders all sell at once, which is why gold and bitcoin fell alongside chips.

The cross-asset picture is starting to change. Treasuries finally acted as a hedge, with the 10-year back below 5% and December hike odds slipping to about 90%; if Wednesday's PCE data are soft, the market may begin to test whether the Fed's tightening cycle ends sooner. Oil is the counterweight: Brent at $92.57 is well below October's peak, but a planned Iranian tanker convoy at Kharg and fresh strikes near Khasab keep a war premium alive, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine's grid pushed European gas up 6%.

This week is short and thin. Flash PMIs on Monday, Dell and HP on Tuesday, PCE and GDP on Wednesday and the Thanksgiving break leave little liquidity to absorb further forced selling. Watch whether Asian chip markets stabilise on Monday, whether Nvidia's after-hours bounce holds, how Bayer trades after its Roundup approval, and whether India keeps drawing the foreign money leaving Taiwan and Korea.

stories.headline: Seventh Straight Loss Puts Wall Street in Correction as the S&P 500 Sinks 3.6% and the Nasdaq 5%
stories.summary: The S&P 500 fell 260.93 points, or 3.64%, to 6,914.90 on Friday, its seventh consecutive decline, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,196.71 points (5.01%) to 22,682.49 and the Dow shed 880.40 points (1.79%) to 48,216.66. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF closed about 11.5% below its 6 October record and the Dow ETF about 11.4% below its August peak, leaving both benchmarks in correction territory. The Dow ETF lost about 8% over the week, its worst week since March 2020. The VIX jumped 7.45 points to 35.89, its highest close since April 2025. A reported SEC review of Nvidia's accounting and a weak second session for Anthropic set off broad liquidation across AI hardware, crypto and even gold.
stories.market: Chips and AI infrastructure led the losses while Treasuries were the only broad haven: the 10-year yield fell 12bp to 4.92%. Defensive staples and health insurers rose, and Nvidia, AMD and QQQ bounced 1.5%-3.6% in after-hours trade.

body: Friday's selling was concentrated in the companies most tied to AI spending. Nvidia fell 14% to $125.53 on volume of about 620 million shares after a Reuters report that SEC staff are examining its accounting, and the Nasdaq 100 tracker QQQ lost 5.67%, against 3.64% for SPY and 1.98% for DIA.

The drop extended a week-long unwind that began with doubts over whether huge AI infrastructure budgets will earn their keep. Anthropic, which debuted on Thursday at an $83 offer price, slid 8.5% to $88.91 on its second day, removing a hoped-for catalyst for the sector.

Strategists were split on what comes next. BNP Paribas's Bénédicte Lowe characterised the move as panic selling, while Deutsche Bank's Binky Chadha said the market was very oversold. Schwab noted that the average Nasdaq stock was already 15% below its high before Friday.

The volatility curve inverted, with the three-month VIX at 30.94 below the spot index, a sign traders were paying up for near-term protection. Rate-hike talk from Fed officials and criticism of the Fed from President Trump and Treasury Secretary Bessent added to the noise, though Treasuries rallied hard.
After the bell, Zscaler jumped 16.3% on reports of takeover talks with CrowdStrike, which fell 4.8%, and chip stocks recovered part of the day's fall.

stories.headline: Micron, Broadcom and Sandisk Sink Double Digits as the Chip Index Drops 10.7%
stories.summary: The Philadelphia Semiconductor index fell 10.7%, which Bloomberg called its worst showing since 2001. Micron lost 13.9%, Broadcom 12.2% to $304.41 after a Ming-Chi Kuo survey said Google had cut 2027 TPU orders (Google has not confirmed), and Sandisk 16.1%. The damage spread across the AI build-out: Nebius fell 16.1%, CoreWeave 12.0%, Lumentum 13.9%, Arista 11.6% and Dell 11.0%, while power suppliers Bloom Energy (-15.3%), Vertiv (-10.1%) and GE Vernova (-7.5%) also slumped. Crypto-linked names Bitmine (-13.9%), Strategy (-9.7%) and Robinhood (-9.4%) fell with bitcoin.
stories.market: Money moved into defensives: General Mills rose 3.7%, McCormick 3.4%, UnitedHealth 2.8% and Walmart 1.5%, and application software such as IBM and Atlassian held up. US-listed Taiwan and Korea funds fell 11% and 8.4%.

body: Friday's chip rout went well beyond Nvidia and AMD, which other pages of this edition cover. Memory, networking, optical and server makers all lost more than 10%, and Taiwan's ASE Technology (-13.8%), TSMC (-9.5%) and UMC (-10.2%) fell sharply in New York trading.
Broadcom's slide came on a supply-chain survey by analyst Ming-Chi Kuo suggesting Google had reduced 2027 orders for its custom TPU chips; Google has not confirmed the claim.

The selling reached companies that supply electricity and cooling to data centres, a sign investors were cutting the whole AI capital-spending trade rather than rotating within it. Caterpillar fell 5.0%.
The defensive bid was notable: packaged-food makers, health insurers and Walmart rose, while big software names such as Salesforce, ServiceNow and Adobe dipped less than 2%.

The pre-market signal was weak: GIFT Nifty futures traded at 25,315.50, down 218 points, after Wall Street's Thursday slide and Asia's early losses. Buying in large financials reversed that. Kotak Mahindra Bank and HDFC Bank each rose about 3%, Maruti Suzuki 2.8%, UltraTech Cement 2.7% and Bajaj Finance 2.4%.

On the week the Sensex gained 2,327.26 points (2.85%) from 81,592.45 and the Nifty 656.30 points (2.61%) from 25,144.30. By sector, banks rose 5.9%, financials 3.7% and autos 3.1%, while metals lost 3%.

Market commentary credited record foreign inflows from investors looking for markets with little AI exposure, a sharp fall in crude this month and solid corporate earnings. The rupee led Asian currencies on Friday morning and settled at 93.32 per dollar after trading as strong as 92.82.

Taiwan's Taiex fell 6.23% to 36,033.29, leaving it about 17.5% down for the week, its worst since 1991; South Korea's Kospi lost 5.21% to 4,869.96 and Japan's Nikkei 225 slid 5.06% to 56,436.65, down 7.7% on the week. stories.market: AI hardware names took the heaviest losses, with SoftBank Group down 14.48%, Advantest 10.32%, Samsung Electronics 7.01% and TSMC 4.76%. The yen firmed to about 159.1 per dollar at the Tokyo close as investors sought safety.

body: The sell-off that began on Wall Street reached its peak in Asia on Friday. Investors cut their holdings of chipmakers, equipment makers and AI-linked groups across the region after Anthropic's market debut failed to restore confidence in AI spending.

Taipei was hit hardest. The Taiex opened at 37,646.13, touched 35,738.68 and closed 2,393.60 points lower at 36,033.29, on turnover of NT$877.35bn. Seoul's Kospi fell 5.21% to 4,869.96, its lowest close since 20 January, and the Kosdaq lost 5.71%.

In Tokyo the Nikkei 225 fell 5.06% to 56,436.65, its lowest close since 13 April, and lost 7.7% on the week; the broader Topix dropped 3.88% to 3,674.22. SoftBank Group fell 14.48%, Kioxia 11.66%, Advantest 10.32% and Tokyo Electron 7.06%.

Greater China held up better because its markets have less exposure to AI hardware. The Hang Seng fell about 1.8-1.9% to roughly 22,421, and mainland China's CSI 300 lost 0.76% to about 3,955. Jakarta's composite fell 0.92%.

Rajat Agarwal, Asia equity strategist at Societe Generale, said markets fear AI's fastest growth phase may be over, and Union Bancaire Privee's Carlos Casanova called the move a collapse of confidence in the AI investment case (Al Jazeera, 20 Nov).

stories.headline: Cook and Paulson Back More Hikes, but the Rout Trims December Odds to About 90% and Kills the Half-Point Bet
stories.summary: Fed Governor Lisa Cook, speaking in Chile on Friday, said delaying rate increases risks leaving the Fed behind the curve and explained her vote for a hike in October. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said she favours raising rates in a deliberate way and is open to back-to-back moves, but did not endorse a half-point step. Futures priced about a 90% chance of a 25bp December hike by Friday's close, down from about 99% on CME FedWatch earlier in the day, with almost nothing left on Christopher Waller's 50bp call. Markets see the policy rate peaking near 4.47% by October 2027, from a 3.88% effective rate today. The University of Michigan's final November sentiment reading rose to 51.5 from 48 in October.
stories.market: The repricing pulled the 2-year yield down 13bp to 4.63%, and the January hike probability fell to about 56% from 67% on Thursday. President Trump and Treasury Secretary Bessent both criticised the hiking path.

sources.name: Fortune: Waller and Cook on hikes

body: Cook said she had preferred a rate increase at the October meeting, citing inflation that has run above the 2% target for more than five and a half years and the risk that wage and price setters start to expect it to stay high.

Paulson's remarks around midday in New York leaned the same way, but stopped short of the half-point move Waller floated on Wednesday. Waller, who appeared early on Friday, made no new policy comment.

The target range is 3.75%-4.00% after a September hike, the first in more than three years. A 25bp move on 9 December would lift it to 4.00%-4.25%. October minutes released on 18 November showed staff warning that long-run inflation expectations may have become unanchored.
Friday's equity crash cut hike odds only modestly, suggesting traders still see inflation, not markets, as the deciding factor. Trump said rates are high because of what he called a political Fed.

stories.summary: ECB President Christine Lagarde has said she cannot guarantee a rate increase at the 17 December meeting, even with euro-area inflation confirmed at 4.0% for October, a three-year high, and core inflation revised up to 2.6%. Markets still lean towards a hike from the 2.50% deposit rate. Bond markets rallied with Treasuries on Friday: Germany's 10-year yield fell 8.8bp over the week to 3.302%, and the UK 10-year 9.5bp to 5.243%. body: The final October inflation figures from Eurostat confirmed headline inflation at 4.0% and nudged core up to 2.6%, keeping pressure on the ECB to follow the Fed in tightening.

Lagarde's refusal to pre-commit leaves the December decision tied to the flash November inflation data due on 1 December and the staff projections. The deposit rate stands at 2.50%; a hike would take it to 2.75%.
In the UK, October retail sales rose 0.7%, beating forecasts of no change, as consumers stockpiled, while consumer confidence improved to -22. Gilt yields still fell with global bonds.
Across the region, 10-year yields fell on the day and the week: France 5.7bp to 4.872%, Spain 3.2bp to 3.906% and Italy 2.1bp to 4.408% for the week.

stories.headline: Hormuz Mine Strikes Turn Oil Higher: Brent Settles at $92.57 After WTI Erases a $5 Drop
stories.summary: Brent crude for January settled up 59 cents, or 0.64%, at $92.57 a barrel on Friday, and WTI for December rose 77 cents (0.93%) to $83.98. WTI had been down nearly $5 a barrel early in the session before reports that two tankers struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, with Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy saying the ships were burning. Even so, both benchmarks posted weekly losses, about 5% for WTI and nearly 4% for Brent. US natural gas jumped 5.35% to $3.443 per million BTU.
stories.market: Oil held up while equities and other commodities sold off, helping energy stocks outperform. A third US carrier in the region and Houthi warnings to Saudi Red Sea ports kept a risk premium in prices.

sources.name: OK Energy Today: Friday gain in oil prices

body: The session swung on headlines from the Gulf. Selling in the morning tracked the wider risk-off move and worries about ample supply, before the mine reports and signs of a more forward-leaning US military posture sent crude back into positive territory.
The Houthis urged people near Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports to leave and told shipping companies to pull vessels, adding to concerns over the Bab el-Mandeb route.
Some buying was also tied to positioning ahead of next week's US Thanksgiving holiday. Brent has still fallen steeply in November, from much higher levels earlier in the autumn.

stories.headline: Gold Drops to a 14-Month Low Near $3,514 and Heads for Its Worst Week Since March
stories.summary: Gold fell for a fifth straight session on Friday, with spot touching $3,513.54 an ounce, its lowest since September 2025. body: The slide accelerated as falling equities forced investors to raise cash, a pattern seen in past sell-offs when gold initially drops alongside risk assets.

stories.headline: Carney Leans on Beijing as the US-Canada Trade War Drags Into Its Fourth Month
stories.summary: Talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed in August and both sides have since imposed heavy retaliatory tariffs, with steel, aluminium and autos at the centre of the dispute. A Carney-Trump meeting on the APEC sidelines in Shenzhen on 19 November produced only a pledge to keep talking. Two days earlier, on 17 November, Canada signed a new pact with China that gives Canadian farm and food exports further tariff relief in exchange for a two-year extension of tariff exemptions on some Chinese steel and aluminium. That builds on a January deal letting up to 49,000 Chinese EVs into Canada at a 6.1% tariff instead of 100%. Trade experts quoted by TIME say the China option gives Ottawa some leverage, but the US remains by far its biggest market, taking C$683.3 billion of Canadian exports in 2025.
stories.market: With no deal in sight, tariff risk stays priced into North American autos, steel and aluminium, and the Canadian dollar. Canola, pork and LNG exporters gain from the China channel, and the steel exemptions could anger Washington.

body: Canada's partnership with China dates from January 2026, when Ottawa allowed up to 49,000 Chinese EVs at a 6.1% tariff and Beijing cut duties on Canadian canola seed and other farm goods. Trump criticised that deal at the time.

In the US-Canada dispute, each side accuses the other of going back on earlier commitments on metals and autos, and Trump has said the US holds all the cards. Carney replies that Canada's leverage is its relationships with other countries.

Ottawa has been signing deals elsewhere. On 14 November it concluded free-trade negotiations with the 11-member ASEAN bloc and separately with the Philippines. The EU proposed in September that Canada become an associate member, and an October summit in Montreal confirmed that plan.

Carney stresses that Canada's China trade is mostly commodities such as canola, pork, halibut, LNG and oil, not advanced chips. Critics at home, including Ontario Premier Doug Ford, oppose letting in more Chinese EVs, and Conservative MP Michael Chong has raised national-security concerns.

Academics quoted by TIME say geography and car-parts supply chains, in which parts cross the border about six times before final assembly, make any quick shift away from the US unrealistic. They add that the steel and aluminium carve-out for China could irritate US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

stories.summary: President Trump said on Friday that interest rates are too high because of a very political Fed, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticised calls for a larger December move. stories.headline: Iran War, Day 267: Tehran Readies a Tanker Convoy to Test the US Blockade as Another Ship Burns Off Khasab
stories.summary: More than 14 Iranian tankers have gathered near Kharg Island, most with transponders switched off, according to Al-Monitor as cited by Iran International on 20 November; Guards-linked outlets say dozens are preparing to sail for China, which would be Iran's first seaborne crude export since mid-July. No Iranian official has confirmed the plan, and Fars warned that any interference would bring strikes on oil facilities in six Gulf states. On 20 November UKMTO said an outbound tanker was hit by an unknown projectile 8 nautical miles north of Khasab and caught fire, while Iranian media reported a missile strike on Qeshm Island. Trump told Israel's Channel 12 he is 'not rushing' and could wait until after the new year, and the Senate rejected a war-powers resolution 48-51.
stories.market: Brent settled up 59 cents at $92.57 on 20 November, its third straight weekly loss and about 21% below its 30 October close, as convoy threats and Houthi warnings to Saudi Red Sea ports offset surplus talk; WTI settled at $83.98. Tanker owners, war-risk underwriters (a US official put cover at $64m per transit, an unverified figure), Gulf equities and Asian LNG buyers carry the most direct exposure.

body: Day 267 of the war brings the clearest sign yet that Tehran wants to break the economic stalemate. Al-Monitor reported more than 14 Iranian tankers massed near Kharg Island, most running dark, and Guards-linked channels spoke of dozens readying for China. Iran's seaborne crude exports have been halted since mid-July; Kpler recorded no loadings at all in September, and output has fallen to about 1.8m barrels a day, roughly half its pre-war level. Kpler expects payments for the last cargoes by mid-December, after which Tehran stands to lose $3bn to $6bn a month, according to Iran International's account of the data.

Washington has tightened rather than loosened its grip. On 18 November Central Command extended the blockade to ship-to-ship transfers at sea, warning that vessels may be boarded, diverted or seized; it says it has redirected 150 merchant ships and disabled five since June. Fars responded that any attack on a convoy would trigger strikes on oil facilities in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain, and a lawmaker noted Iran had 'not yet closed' Bab el-Mandeb.

In the strait itself, UKMTO said on 20 November that an outbound tanker was hit by an unknown projectile 8 nautical miles north of Khasab in Oman's Musandam peninsula and reported a fire on board (warning 214-26); the Revolutionary Guards instead said the ship struck a mine. Iranian media reported a missile hitting Qeshm Island on the northern shore. No casualties were reported in either incident. It follows a week in which tanker attacks around the strait rose sharply.

In Washington, Trump said he was in no rush to decide on wider strikes and could wait until after the new year, while CBS sources said the US and Israel are weighing a new short-term attack because of concern that Iran is rebuilding missile production underground. Iran's foreign ministry rejected Trump's suggestion that it is seeking chemical or biological weapons. The Senate voted 48-51 against a House-passed resolution to limit strikes on Iran. In Israel, opposition figure Avigdor Liberman said there was no security case for striking Iran now.

For markets the cross-currents are visible in the price. Brent rose 0.6% on Friday to $92.57, with traders citing the third US carrier in the region, the tanker incidents and Houthi threats against Saudi Red Sea ports, but it still fell for a third week. UKMTO counted 308 crossings in the week to 11 November, about 65% below pre-war traffic, and S&P Global put war-risk premiums at 7.5-10% of hull value in July against 1-3% before the war.

stories.headline: Saudi Coalition Strikes Hodeidah Port; Houthis Threaten Jeddah and Every Saudi Red Sea Harbour
stories.summary: The Saudi-led coalition said on 20 November it struck the operational capabilities of Hodeidah port after telling civilians to leave, along with targets in Sanaa, Saada and Taiz in what Al Jazeera's correspondent called the heaviest strikes of the conflict. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree replied that Jeddah and all Saudi Red Sea ports would become targets, told workers and residents to leave and urged shipping lines to pull their vessels out. The Houthis also warned airlines away from Saudi airspace and claimed attacks on the Shuqaiq power station and Jazan port; the coalition said it intercepted missiles and drones aimed at the south. Houthi authorities said 19 people were killed when Saudi forces hit a boat, a claim not independently confirmed.
stories.market: Oil traders cited the Houthi threat to Saudi Red Sea ports in Friday's Brent gain to $92.57: with Hormuz constrained, Yanbu and the East-West pipeline are Saudi Arabia's main export bypass. Freight to Jeddah, Saudi equities and Egypt's tentative Suez recovery are the direct channels; Air India extended flight cancellations to the kingdom.

body: The war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis escalated sharply on 20 November. After warning civilians to evacuate the port area, the Saudi-led coalition said it hit Hodeidah's capacity to move weapons and ballistic missiles, and reported further operations against missile and drone sites in Sanaa as well as in Saada and Taiz governorates.

The Houthis answered with the most direct threat yet to Saudi Arabia's western seaboard. Their military spokesman said Jeddah and all Saudi Red Sea ports would become targets, urged workers and nearby residents to leave and told shipping companies to move their ships. They also told airlines to avoid Saudi airspace except near Mecca and Medina and claimed strikes on the Shuqaiq power station and Jazan port. The coalition said it intercepted ballistic missiles over Jazan and destroyed drones over Riyadh and the south; Syria and Pakistan condemned the Houthi attacks.

The escalation follows the 19 November missile attack that damaged a tower in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District. On the ground, government forces in Aden are preparing to defend their last major stronghold as the Houthis advance along the coast, and Taiz is now cut off from Aden, with residents reporting shortages of water and fuel.

The commercial stakes are high because the Red Sea coast is Saudi Arabia's main outlet while Hormuz is disrupted: the East-West pipeline to Yanbu carries about 4m barrels a day and was struck on 9 November. Container lines had only just begun to return to Suez; Egypt's canal revenue reached $724m in October, the highest since 2023.

stories.headline: Six Killed in Gaza Strikes After Central Push Ends; Israel Hits Hezbollah Site in Beqaa
stories.summary: Israeli strikes killed six people in central Gaza on 20 November, according to the territory's civil defence agency, a day after the army ended a tank-backed operation beyond the Yellow Line; the military said it targeted militants. More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire by an AFP tally of health ministry data, and Israel says seven soldiers and a contractor have died. The Board of Peace overseeing the truce told the UN Security Council that a ceasefire delivering nothing visible cannot last. In Lebanon, Israel said it hit the entrances of a Hezbollah weapons site near Janta in the Beqaa, its second strike in the east that week.
stories.market: These fronts reach markets through regional risk premia: Israeli assets and the shekel, Lebanese debt and East Mediterranean gas. Israeli politics add a domestic channel after Netanyahu lost his Knesset majority, with Benny Eisenkot holding the mandate to form a government.

body: Gaza's civil defence agency said six people were killed in Israeli strikes on 20 November: four in an air strike southwest of the Bureij camp and two in drone strikes in Deir al-Balah and north of Nuseirat. The Israeli military told AFP it had targeted several militants. The strikes came a day after the army completed a ground operation with tanks beyond the Yellow Line in central Gaza, which it said was aimed at a tunnel.

The truce that took effect in October 2025 formally holds, but its overseers are increasingly blunt. In a report to the UN Security Council on 17 November, the US-backed Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and conditions on the ground is the main risk, and that Israel has not allowed its technocratic administration to start work or decided on police training, delaying the international stabilisation force. It also cited supply restrictions and funding gaps as civilians face another winter in tents.

In Lebanon, the Israeli military said it struck the entrances of a site near Janta in the Beqaa Valley on 19 November that Hezbollah had previously used for missile production and storage, and to which it said the group had returned. Lebanon's national news agency reported five air strikes in the east. Israeli forces still hold a security zone about 10 km deep along the border, and the US-sponsored framework has stalled over Hezbollah's refusal to disarm.

Israel's political transition adds uncertainty. Netanyahu, who lost his majority in last week's election, again called for a unity government; Eisenkot, who holds the mandate, has refused to join him. Liberman said there was no security justification for striking Iran now.

stories.headline: Russia Hits Kyiv's Bridges and Grid in Revenge Strike as European Gas Jumps 6%
stories.summary: Russia launched an hours-long missile and drone attack overnight into 20 November after Putin vowed retaliation for Ukraine's strikes on the Crimean Bridge, damaging three Dnipro bridges in Kyiv and cutting power in parts of five city districts. Ukraine's prime minister said eight people were killed and 28 injured nationwide, and emergency blackouts hit Lviv, Ivano-Frankivsk and Zakarpattia; a Kh-101 cruise missile fell in southeastern Poland. Germany, France, the UK and Ukraine proposed a winter energy and Black Sea shipping truce, which Putin rejected. Ukraine's strikes on Russian refining continue, with Reuters sources putting the cut in runs at about 45% in November.
stories.market: Dutch TTF gas rose about 6% to €89.54/MWh on 20 November on a Norwegian Troll outage, colder forecasts and EU storage at 69.8%, nearly triple year-earlier prices. Lost Russian refining supports diesel, and European defence names trade on the stalled ceasefire track and new EU funding for Ukraine.

body: Russia's overnight assault into 20 November, using ballistic and cruise missiles launched in part from Tu-160 bombers, followed Putin's promise of a response 'far more painful' than Ukraine's attacks on the Crimean Bridge. In Kyiv the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Southern bridges were damaged; about 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro in the city each day. Officials reported six dead in Kyiv, several of them water-utility workers, and eight across the country, including two at a Lviv railway station.

The energy system took further hits as winter sets in. DTEK reported outages in five Kyiv districts, emergency blackouts were imposed in three western regions and around Dnipro, and in Kryvyi Rih boiler houses, water pumps and hospitals moved to generators. A Russian Kh-101 missile came down in southeastern Poland. Germany, France, the UK and Ukraine have called for an energy and Black Sea shipping ceasefire for the winter; Putin said Russia would not negotiate such truces.

Ukraine's campaign against Russian energy continues. Its forces have struck the Kerch Bridge rail span repeatedly since 16 November, and refineries and depots in the south and along the Volga. Reuters industry sources say Ukrainian drones cut Russian refinery runs by about 45% in November. Russia's defence ministry said it intercepted 4,305 Ukrainian drones in 48 hours.

Diplomacy remains split. After the 19 November Shenzhen summit, Putin said he and Trump still backed the Alaska proposals, under which Ukraine would cede the part of Donbas it holds and stay out of NATO, and Medvedev said 'no-one needs Europe'. The EU has agreed to raise €45bn toward Ukraine's projected €70bn shortfall next year, including €25bn for military aid, and troops from 11 countries began the Koalicja 26.2 exercise in Poland on 20 November to prepare for a post-ceasefire mission.

In gas, the Dutch TTF front month rose about 6% to €89.54 per MWh on 20 November as a Troll field outage cut Norwegian flows to 290m cubic metres a day on 19 November and forecasts turned colder; EU storage stood at 69.8% against 81.2% a year earlier.

stories.headline: RSF and SPLM-N Claim Gains Near Damazin as Sudan's War Opens a Blue Nile Front
stories.summary: The RSF-SPLM-N alliance said on 19 November it had captured the Bau locality headquarters, about 60 km southwest of Damazin, the Blue Nile state capital, and Village 12, about 40 km from the city; a local civil-society figure confirmed the claim, and the army said it repelled a separate attack on the Kurmuk front. The push comes as the army advances in West Kordofan around Al-Khuway. Amnesty International said nine RSF drone strikes on El Obeid between June and August killed 37 civilians and should be investigated as war crimes. About 11.4 million people are forcibly displaced.
stories.market: Sudan's war is financed partly by gold, so the conflict feeds gold flows through neighbouring states; bullion itself fell about 8% this week on Fed hike bets, to about $3,558 spot on 20 November. Fighting near Damazin also bears on Blue Nile hydropower and regional trade via Port Sudan.

body: The front in Sudan's war widened to the southeast this week. The RSF and its SPLM-N ally said on 19 November that they had captured the headquarters of Bau locality in the Ingessana Hills, about 60 km southwest of Damazin, the capital of Blue Nile state, along with Village 12 on the Geissan front about 40 km from the city. A local civil-society figure confirmed the claim to Radio Tamazuj; the army could not be reached, and its division in Damazin said it had repelled an attack on the Kurmuk front.

In Kordofan the momentum has favoured the army: in the days before, it said it had cleared villages around Al-Khuway and toward Al-Nuhud and Abu Zabad in West Kordofan. El Obeid, the North Kordofan capital and the hub between RSF-held west and army-held centre, remains partially besieged by the RSF after nearly two years.

Amnesty International said on 18 November that nine RSF drone strikes on El Obeid between June and August killed 37 civilians and hit residential areas, the city's power plant, fuel stations and the main market, and called for them to be investigated as war crimes. The UN refugee agency counts about 11.4 million people forcibly displaced.

The market channel is mainly gold, a key source of war finance traded through neighbouring states, along with trade through Port Sudan and Blue Nile's hydropower. Gold futures were already falling before this week's Fed-driven slide, which took spot bullion to about $3,558 an ounce on 20 November.

stories.headline: IG Metall's First Full-Day Strikes in Eight Years Halt BMW as VW Seeks a Two-Year Pay Freeze
stories.summary: IG Metall began full-day warning strikes in Bavaria's metal and electrical industry on Friday 20 November, its first of this kind in eight years, demanding 5% more pay. No cars were built at BMW's Dingolfing plant, and production at BMW Landshut and Munich and at Audi Ingolstadt was set to stop for the day after night shifts at suppliers Benteler, Linamar and Bosch Rexroth were halted. Volkswagen, in demands sent to the union on 19 November, asked for no pay rises in 2027 and 2028, an end to a bonus worth 27.5% of monthly pay and more flexible weekly hours; talks covering about 130,000 staff start on 24 November in Emden. Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 full-time jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs after a €180 million operating loss in the first nine months of 2026. The DAX fell 2.60% on Friday to 24,801.22, ending its worst week since March 2025 with a 7.29% loss.
stories.market: Lost output and rising wage tension add to pressure on German carmakers and suppliers already hit by the global sell-off; Lufthansa's cuts point to cost pressure in European aviation.

sources.name: Life in Germany: jobs briefing, 20 Nov
investingLive: European stocks end a bruising week

body: The Bavarian strikes started late on Thursday with night shifts at Benteler in Schwandorf, Linamar in Penzberg and Bosch Rexroth in Elchingen. IG Metall describes Dingolfing as BMW's largest plant in Europe.

Volkswagen's in-house agreement is separate from the regional metalworking contract. Besides the pay freeze, VW wants to drop a monthly allowance of €167 and move away from the 35-hour week without extra pay for longer hours. IG Metall strongly rejected the demands. The peace obligation runs until 31 December, after which warning strikes at VW are possible.

Lufthansa's plan was set out in an internal letter from chief executive Jens Ritter and four other board members, reported by dpa and tagesschau. The airline also wants to cut short- and medium-haul capacity and replace part of its Airbus A320 fleet with A220s. Timing and method of the job cuts are still open.
German government bonds rallied as equities fell: the 10-year Bund yield closed at 3.302% on Friday, down 9.5 basis points on the day and 8.8 bp on the week.

stories.headline: Commerzbank Lifts Its 2026 Profit Goal to €3.5 Billion as UniCredit Nears Control
stories.summary: A day after UniCredit and Berlin settled their main differences over the takeover, Commerzbank chief executive Bettina Orlopp raised the bank's 2026 net profit forecast to €3.5 billion from at least €3.4 billion, Reuters reported on Friday. Orlopp welcomed the clarity on the Frankfurt headquarters and the stock listing, though the strategy of the combined bank, including UniCredit's wish to shrink Commerzbank's international network, still has to be worked out. UniCredit holds 47.59% of Commerzbank's capital and 49.65% of voting rights from its exchange offer of 0.485 new UniCredit shares per Commerzbank share, but does not yet control the bank. Both stocks fell with the market on Friday: a MarketScreener snapshot showed Commerzbank at €36.48 (-2.13%) and UniCredit at €78.41 (-2.38%).
stories.market: The upgrade supports Commerzbank's value in the share exchange; remaining approvals in Poland and under the EU foreign-subsidies rules are the last hurdles before settlement, after which UniCredit plans to reshape the supervisory board.

sources.name: Reuters via MarketScreener: Commerzbank raises outlook
Reuters via Manila Times: UniCredit-Germany deal
FinTech Weekly: Brussels clears the takeover

body: Under the deal set out in Andrea Orcel's 18 November letter to Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, the merged bank's German arm stays in Frankfurt as a listed entity, Berlin drops its demand for two supervisory board seats and UniCredit adds Germans to its own board. Klingbeil said Berlin supports a swift process and an orderly transfer of control.
The European Commission cleared the deal without conditions on 16 November, and the US Federal Reserve approved it the same day. The ECB had allowed UniCredit to go above 30% on 15 October.

UniCredit expects the remaining clearances, from Poland's financial regulator and under the EU Foreign Subsidies Regulation, in late November, followed by settlement. It then plans to call an extraordinary general meeting to replace supervisory board members, with new governance and a Commerzbank Unlocked plan in the first quarter of 2027.
The combined group would hold more than €1.3 trillion of assets. Commerzbank staff have long opposed the deal, partly because of Orcel's plans to cut jobs in Germany.

stories.headline: Klingbeil Opens a Two-Year Consultation on How to Restart German Growth
stories.summary: Germany's finance ministry opened a call for workshop proposals on Friday 20 November for a dialogue process on how to secure growth and what role forward-looking fiscal policy can play, Reuters reported. The ministry is working through 12 topics, including tax, investment and domestic demand, industrial policy, the energy transition, trade and sovereignty, and housing. Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil will open the process on 2 December with economists from around the world; workshops follow in the first half of 2027, and a white paper with recommendations up to 2035 is due in 2028. The launch came as Bund yields fell, with the 10-year closing at 3.302% on Friday, down 9.5 basis points.
stories.market: The process sets no new spending figures, so it is unlikely to move Bunds on its own; investors are watching for signs of fiscal support as German industry weakens.

stories.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham met European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on Friday 20 November for the second UK-EU summit, after the first in London in May 2025. The agenda covered security, illegal migration and crime, and cutting red tape and costs for farmers and food businesses. Separately, the Rio Times noted that the EU-Mercosur trade agreement looks unlikely to be ratified soon.
stories.market: Easier food and farm trade rules would help UK and EU agri-food exporters; the euro was at $1.0984 and sterling at $1.3110 on Friday.

stories.headline: India Becomes the Shelter From the AI Storm as Foreign Buying Hits a Record $12.2bn
stories.summary: Foreign investors have bought a record $12.21bn of Indian equities in November as of 20 Nov, as funds rotate out of AI-heavy Asian markets into one with little exposure to chips. The shift showed on Friday: the Nifty 50 rose 1.12% to a nine-month high of 25,800.60 while the MSCI Asia-Pacific index fell 3.3%. Over the week Indian bank shares gained 5.9% and financials 3.7%. Goldman Sachs upgraded India to overweight on 19 Nov with a December 2027 Nifty target of 28,500, about 10.5% above Friday's close.
stories.market: Inflows are concentrated in large private banks and financials and are supporting the rupee, which led Asian currencies on Friday and settled at 93.32 per dollar; IT exporters remain the weak spot because they are tied to US tech spending.

sources.name: The Week: Indian equities at nine-month highs

body: November is now the largest month on record for foreign buying of Indian shares. The Week put the month-to-date total at $12.21bn on 20 Nov, up from about $11.28bn through 18 Nov reported in market round-ups a day earlier.

The flows reflect a wider rotation. As chip and AI stocks fell across Taiwan, South Korea and Japan this week, India, whose index has few hardware makers, became a destination for regional funds. On Friday the Nifty rose 1.12% while the MSCI Asia-Pacific index fell 3.3% and was heading for an 8.5% weekly loss.

Lower oil prices are also helping: Brent has fallen sharply this month on hopes of easing Middle East tensions, according to The Week, which cuts India's import bill and supports the rupee. The rupee touched 92.82 per dollar intraday on Friday before settling at 93.32.

Demand for India exposure offshore is also rising. Open interest in GIFT Nifty futures reached a record $22.21bn (about ₹2.07 lakh crore) on 18 Nov, above the previous high of $21.84bn set on 23 Oct, CNBC-TV18 reported.
Goldman Sachs upgraded India to overweight on 19 Nov and set a December 2027 Nifty target of 28,500, reported in the previous edition.

stories.headline: Coal India's ₹8,981 Crore Mahanadi Sale Is Only 0.42 Times Covered on Day Two
stories.summary: State-owned Coal India's sale of about 10% of Mahanadi Coalfields, an offer for sale worth up to ₹8,981 crore at ₹129-136 a share, was 0.42 times subscribed by 12:04 on 20 Nov, its second day. Institutions bid for 1.26 times their portion, but retail investors took up only 0.20 times and non-institutional investors 0.12 times. The issue closes on 23 Nov and is due to list on 27 Nov; Coal India, not Mahanadi, receives the money.
stories.market: Weak retail demand for a large state-company share sale contrasts with record foreign buying of listed Indian stocks; the final tally on Monday is a gauge for Coal India shares and for appetite for future state stake sales.

stories.headline: Hong Kong Slides Again as Inflation Beats Forecasts; Mainland Shares Hold Up Better
stories.summary: The Hang Seng fell about 1.8-1.9% on Friday 20 Nov to roughly 22,421, after a 1.95% drop on Thursday, keeping it close to bear-market territory about 20% below its 29 January peak. Hong Kong's October consumer prices rose 2.2% from a year earlier, above the 2.0% forecast and up from 1.9% in September. Mainland China's CSI 300 lost only 0.76% to about 3,955, and the onshore yuan was steady at about 6.6665 per dollar. Beijing left its one-year and five-year loan prime rates at 3.0% and 3.5% on Friday, unchanged for an 18th month.
stories.market: Mainland A-shares, with little AI-hardware weight, are acting as a relative refuge, while Hong Kong's tech-heavy index tracks the global sell-off; firmer local inflation reduces room for Hong Kong rate relief, a headwind for property stocks.

body: Hong Kong extended its losses on Friday. Rio Times data show the Hang Seng down 1.84% at about 22,421, and Al Jazeera put its fall at 1.9%; that follows Thursday's 1.95% drop to 22,841.62.

stories.headline: Judge gives final approval to Bayer's $7.25 billion Roundup settlement
stories.summary: St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer granted final approval on Friday 20 November to the $7.25 billion class settlement Bayer's Monsanto unit proposed in February to resolve current and future US claims that Roundup weedkiller causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Bayer will pay into a fund for up to 21 years. Average payouts range from about $10,000 to $165,000 depending on exposure, age at diagnosis and severity, and the total includes $600 million in attorneys' fees. The judge called the terms fair, reasonable and adequate, overruled objections that payouts were too low, and noted that Bayer risked bankruptcy if the deal failed. Bayer faced about 65,000 claims in US courts, and roughly 200 federal cases sit outside the settlement, according to the company. Bayer still denies that glyphosate causes cancer.
stories.market: The ruling came after European markets closed on Friday, so Bayer (BAYN.DE) shares react on Monday. It removes the biggest single uncertainty over a stock that has lost 46% since the $63 billion Monsanto purchase in 2018, per Reuters.

body: Judge Timothy Boyer of the St. Louis Circuit Court signed a written judgment on Friday 20 November approving the nationwide class settlement. It covers people already diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma after Roundup exposure and people who are diagnosed in future, provided their exposure came before the deal was proposed in February 2026.

Payments come through annual contributions to a fund that can run for up to 21 years. Average awards are tiered: long-exposed farm, industrial or turf workers diagnosed with an aggressive form before age 60 could average up to about $165,000, while those diagnosed at 78 or older would average about $10,000, according to the AP. St. Louis Public Radio reported a separate $1 billion security fund against funding shortfalls and more than $400 million set aside for claimants in special circumstances.

Objectors argued the deal locks in future claimants for decades, bars punitive damages and leaves the product on sale. The judge overruled them, saying delay would leave victims, some terminally ill, waiting indefinitely. He described the deal as among the largest mass-tort personal-injury class settlements on record.

The settlement follows a June 2026 US Supreme Court decision, by 7-2, that federal pesticide law bars state-law failure-to-warn claims, overturning a $1.25 million jury award to Missouri resident John Durnell. Plaintiffs' lawyer Christopher Seeger said that ruling narrowed victims' options in court. In October a Missouri jury sided with Bayer in the first Roundup trial after the Supreme Court ruling.

Bayer CEO Bill Anderson called the approval a decisive milestone in containing the litigation. The company had already set aside $16 billion for Roundup legal costs before this deal, per the AP, and had previously settled much of the litigation for $10.9 billion in 2020. The order can still be appealed.

stories.headline: New York Times must face narrowed version of Trump's $15 billion defamation suit
stories.summary: US District Judge Steven Merryday in Tampa on Thursday 19 November denied The New York Times Co.'s motion to dismiss President Donald Trump's $15 billion defamation suit over three articles and the book Lucky Loser, published by Penguin Random House. The judge dismissed two claims, narrowed four and struck more than two dozen challenged statements, leaving claims over passages that Trump says accused him of tax fraud, tax evasion or money laundering. He found Trump had adequately alleged actual malice at this early stage; the ruling is not a finding that the Times defamed him. The Times stands by its reporting and may appeal.

stories.headline: Singaporean accused of leading global insider-trading ring appears in Boston court
stories.summary: Zhi Ge, a 35-year-old Singaporean, made his first appearance in federal court in Boston on Friday 20 November after being extradited from Singapore to face securities fraud and money-laundering charges. Prosecutors say he led, with a former France-based investment banker who remains a fugitive, a network of nine people that made tens of millions of dollars trading on confidential deal information from 2016 to 2024. Deals cited include AstraZeneca's $39 billion purchase of Alexion in 2020 and Novartis's $2.9 billion takeover of MorphoSys in 2024. Ge was arrested in Singapore in 2024; his lawyer says he will plead not guilty at arraignment on 16 December.
stories.market: The case shows cross-border enforcement reaching pre-announcement trading in pharma and biotech takeover targets, a sector where M&A leaks move option and share prices.

stories.headline: CFTC loses emergency bid to stop New York policing Kalshi, as courts keep siding with states
stories.summary: US District Judge Lorna Schofield in Manhattan on Friday 20 November denied the CFTC's emergency request to block New York Attorney General Letitia James from pursuing her case against prediction-market operator Kalshi, saying the agency had not shown it was likely to win its argument that federal law pre-empts state gambling rules. A day earlier another judge had sent James's case, filed on 31 July, back to state court. The ruling follows a 2-1 decision by the Fourth Circuit on 18 November that Maryland can apply its sports-wagering laws to Kalshi, the third of four federal appeals rulings to favour states. The CFTC, which treats Kalshi's event contracts as swaps, has sued 12 states to assert exclusive jurisdiction.
stories.market: The string of losses raises legal risk for prediction-market platforms and their sports-betting rivals' competitive position, and makes a Supreme Court showdown more likely.

stories.headline: Trump urges Nvidia to take back Huang as state and federal probes advance
stories.summary: President Donald Trump said on Friday 20 November that he would like Nvidia to give Jensen Huang a second chance as CEO, calling him a good man who made bad decisions and should apologise. Nvidia's board said on 17 November it does not plan to reinstate Huang, who resigned on 12 November. What is new since yesterday: Trump's intervention, a New York Times report on Friday about the alleged spy Alice Huang's family ties to China's defence industry, and scrutiny by Democrats of whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick helped Cantor Fitzgerald, run by his sons, avoid losses linked to the affair; Trump said he retains confidence in Lutnick. California's subpoena of 19 November and an SEC civil probe remain open, and Huang has agreed to closed-door interviews with three House panels in early December. No wrongdoing has been found.
stories.market: Nvidia (NVDA) had fallen more than 10% since Huang's departure as of 17 November, per TechCrunch; political pressure over governance adds uncertainty for the stock and for Chinese AI names such as Alibaba (BABA).

stories.headline: Argentina's Blue Dollar Posts Its Biggest Weekly Jump in Over Two Years; Naira Holds Near ₦1,468 on the Street
stories.summary: Argentina's informal 'blue' dollar closed Friday 20 Nov at a record ARS 1,665 to sell in Ámbito's survey, up ARS 100 on the week and its biggest weekly rise in more than two years; El Cronista quoted ARS 1,675, a 7.4% weekly gain. The official Banco Nación rate ended at ARS 1,595, while the financial MEP and CCL rates closed at ARS 1,682.79 and ARS 1,790.39, gaps of 6.5% and 13.3% over the official rate, according to Ámbito. In Lagos, street dealers quoted the naira at ₦1,468 per dollar on 20 Nov, little changed from ₦1,470 a day earlier, against about ₦1,352 in early official NFEM trade. Iran's open-market dollar was steady at 2,746,000 rials at 08:35 Tehran time on 21 Nov, up 1.9% in a week.
stories.market: Ámbito says Argentina's central bank broke a nine-session run of dollar purchases on 20 Nov as bonds fell and country risk rose; economists cited by El Cronista point to year-end bonus cash, holiday demand and thin informal volumes. Nigeria's gross reserves stood at $54.71 billion on 18 Nov, down from $55.26 billion on 27 Oct.

body: The blue dollar's climb accelerated through the week: El Cronista put it at ARS 1,560 on 13 Nov before Friday's finish around ARS 1,665-1,675. Ámbito said the gap between the blue and the wholesale rate reached its widest since September 2025, and the wholesale rate rose ARS 15 on Friday to ARS 1,580, its largest weekly rise since June.

Analysts quoted by El Cronista tied the move to hedging demand amid doubts over the economic programme and upcoming debt payments, falling Argentine bonds, seasonal demand as year-end bonuses and holidays approach, and thin volumes in informal exchange houses. One economist named the 26 Nov Treasury debt auction and a Senate vote on suspending primary elections as near-term catalysts.

In Nigeria, The Trumpet reported buying quotes of ₦1,445-1,458 and selling at ₦1,468 on 20 Nov, with analysts citing festive-season demand, import bills and weaker autonomous inflows. Iran's open-market rate has risen about 60% in six months and 142% in a year, according to Alanchand data.

stories.summary: The US Treasury on 20 Nov designated four Iranian individuals it accuses of profiting from the country's oil trade, the latest step in Operation Economic Outcast, launched on 24 Aug. Two of them, former Revolutionary Guards intelligence officer Mohammad Javad Bavand and Majid Taj, were listed under Iran's petroleum-sector order for leading efforts to recover oil money held abroad. Treasury said no Iranian oil is on the water outside the US naval blockade and none has been loaded since the operation began, and Secretary Scott Bessent said Tehran may never see revenue from oil already sold.

stories.headline: Three Arrested Over Alleged Smuggling of Tens of Millions of Dollars in Fakes Through LA and Long Beach Ports
stories.summary: Federal agents arrested three Southern California residents who are charged in a nine-count indictment with smuggling counterfeit goods and other contraband from China through the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, MyNewsLA reported on 20 Nov. Prosecutors allege the scheme, run with others from July 2024 to July 2025, moved tens of millions of dollars' worth of goods; the charges include conspiracy, four smuggling counts and four counts of breaking customs seals. The case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the EPA's criminal division. Smuggling counts carry up to 20 years in prison; the defendants are presumed innocent.

stories.headline: Binance Hackers Shift $860 Million of Ether and Step Up Bitcoin Mixing as Freezes Reach $2.85 Billion
stories.summary: Wallets tied to the $6.3-6.4 billion October theft from Binance moved about 488,000 ETH, worth roughly $860 million, out of five addresses this week, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said on 20 Nov, including 197,460 ETH (about $346 million) on Friday alone, per Onchain Lens via Cointelegraph. Elliptic counted at least 2,310 BTC, about $149 million, passed through coinjoin mixing, roughly 90% of it since Tuesday, while the 18,270 BTC taken directly from the exchange has not moved. Its latest tally puts about $2.85 billion frozen and $2.35 billion still in theft-linked wallets; Binance said on 18 Nov it had won a $6.5 billion worldwide freeze order from the Abu Dhabi Global Market Courts. Recoveries returned to victims so far are small: about $32 million, according to on-chain analyst SomaXBT. US investigators and analytics firms attribute the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group.
stories.market: The flows have lifted volumes on cross-chain swap venues such as THORChain, which processed $239 million of swaps in 24 hours on 20 Nov; ether traded near $1,750 late on 20 Nov, down about 3% on the day, though sources do not tie the decline to the transfers.

body: Three weeks after the largest crypto theft on record, the people behind the Binance breach have accelerated efforts to move and disguise the proceeds. Elliptic, which tracks the funds, said on 20 Nov that about 488,000 ETH had left five wallets in recent days, most of it parked in fresh addresses; about $70 million was swapped into bitcoin and mixed within hours.

Bitcoin mixing has picked up sharply. Elliptic counted at least 2,310 BTC run through coinjoin transactions, about 90% of it since Tuesday 17 Nov, and identified the coordinator as Kruw, a service for Wasabi Wallet users; coordinators do not take custody of funds. The mixed coins came from swaps of other stolen assets such as ETH, XRP and SOL rather than from the 18,270 BTC lifted directly from Binance, which remains untouched.

Elliptic estimates very little has yet been cashed out. About $2.85 billion has been frozen by exchanges, issuers and authorities, and about $2.35 billion remains in wallets linked to the theft. Binance said on 18 Nov it had obtained a $6.5 billion worldwide freeze order against the attackers from the Abu Dhabi Global Market Courts, with further orders letting platforms return assets they have already frozen.

Binance has described the October intrusion as a months-long campaign combining malicious software, a fake job interview and compromised internal AI tools that reached its wallet-signing systems. TRM Labs and Chainalysis link it to TraderTraitor, a North Korea-linked group; the FBI attributed the theft to North Korea on 31 Oct.

Separately, the Justice Department and FBI said on 19 Nov that North Korean hackers stole more than $400 million over about 18 months through fake video calls, in an operation investigators named FaceStealer.

stories.headline: SEC, CFTC and Manhattan Prosecutors Charge Backward Hat Capital Founders Over Alleged $560 Million Forex Ponzi
stories.summary: US authorities on 20 Nov unsealed parallel cases against Backward Hat Capital, an Indiana-linked group of forex funds that the SEC says raised more than $560 million from at least 2,000 investors since July 2022. The SEC alleges that over $470 million, more than 83% of the money raised, went to Ponzi-like payouts to earlier investors (over $250 million) and transfers to co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson or their entities (over $220 million), with little or no trading. The SEC won a temporary restraining order and asset freeze; the US Attorney's Office in Manhattan charged Williams and Johnson with securities fraud and conspiracy counts, and the CFTC filed its own complaint. A third man, Joseph Anderson, is accused by the SEC of producing fake audit reports. The charges are allegations and the defendants have not been convicted.
stories.market: The case adds to scrutiny of promoter-sold private funds promising steady monthly returns (the portal showed 6-7% a month); the SEC says accounts held only about $500,000 by 9 Oct 2026, pointing to deep losses for investors.

body: The SEC filed its complaint on 17 Nov in the US District Court for the Southern District of Indiana and announced emergency relief on 20 Nov. It names Backward Hat Capital, co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson's Traders Point Capital and Joseph Anderson, and seeks disgorgement from relief defendants.

According to the SEC, limited-partnership interests in 25 purported Backward Hat funds were sold directly and through promoters with the promise of monthly gross returns above 6%. An investor portal displayed monthly gains of 6.05% to 7.03% between March 2024 and February 2026. The agency says money was commingled and that general partners and promoters received more than $50 million.

The SEC says Anderson drafted audit and quality-of-earnings reports in the name of an entity that was not an accounting firm, and received about $2.5 million of investor money. One fund reported $246 million of assets at the end of July 2025, when its bank account allegedly held $1.

Redemption problems surfaced in September 2026, and by 9 Oct the funds' accounts held about $500,000. Prosecutors in the Southern District of New York charged Williams and Johnson with securities fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit securities fraud; Investment Executive reports DOJ puts the amount raised above $600 million.

stories.headline: Delaware Regulator Says It Was 'Intentionally Misled' Over $21 Billion of Mark Walter Insurer Loans
stories.summary: Delaware's Department of Insurance said on 19 Nov that it had been intentionally misled about loans that Delaware Life and Clear Spring Life, insurers controlled by billionaire Mark Walter, made to other businesses in his TWG Global group, and that it has opened its own investigation alongside federal authorities, according to Bloomberg Law and Beinsure. About $21 billion of investments were misclassified and should have been reported as affiliated assets; the insurers had earlier reported about $1 billion. The regulator said auditors and rating agencies were also misled but did not say who was responsible, and rejected criticism of its oversight. The FBI, SEC and Manhattan US attorney's office are investigating; Walter and the companies deny wrongdoing and no charges have been filed.
stories.market: The case sharpens scrutiny of private-credit-heavy, asset-manager-linked life insurers: S&P, Fitch and A.M. Best have moved Delaware Life to a negative outlook, and some banks paused sales of its annuities in late August.

body: The Delaware Department of Insurance said in a statement on 19 Nov that it, other regulators, the insurers themselves, their auditors and credit rating agencies had all been misled about the true nature of investments at Delaware Life and Clear Spring. It said it was investigating in parallel with federal authorities and pushed back against what it called a run of inaccurate claims about state oversight.

The statement followed reporting by The New York Times on 16 Nov and Bloomberg News on 18 Nov questioning whether state supervisors are keeping up with Wall Street's growing role in life insurance. About $21 billion of loans were reclassified as related-party after subpoenas and internal reviews, including $4.6 billion at Clear Spring, according to Fitch, lifting related-party exposure to about 40% of the portfolios.

InvestmentNews reported on 17 Nov that private credit makes up about 45% of Delaware Life's nearly $42 billion of debt investments, up from 9% in 2014, and that the insurer used 97% of its Federal Home Loan Bank borrowing capacity in 2025. Of $6.3 billion of rated affiliated loans, about 80% were rated BBB or lower.

Group 1001, the insurers' parent, has said its capital and liquidity remain strong. US life insurers held $321 billion of affiliated investments at the end of 2025, about 5% of cash and invested assets, according to the NAIC, which will require standardized disclosure of private investments from year-end 2026 filings.

stories.headline: Anthropic Gives Back Half Its Debut Gain, Closing Day Two at $88.91 as Greenshoe Lifts Raise to $93.5bn
stories.summary: Anthropic's ANT shares fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday 20 Nov, their second trading day, leaving them about 7.1% above the $83 IPO price and roughly 20% below the $111.50 first trade. The stock opened about 9% lower at $88.17 and touched an intraday low of $83.05, just five cents above the offer price, as the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.0%. The same day the IPO formally closed: underwriters exercised the full 147m-share overallotment at $83, adding about $12.2bn and taking gross proceeds to about $93.5bn. Including a concurrent $26bn private placement with chip and cloud partners, total money raised is about $119.5bn. The first lock-up release is scheduled for 15 Dec.
stories.market: ANT's slide tracked a 14% drop in Nvidia and a 5.67% fall in the Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQ); with the greenshoe now fully exercised, stabilisation buying by the underwriters near $83 is limited, putting focus on whether the offer price holds. IG's Chris Beauchamp suggested demand for the new stock may have drained liquidity from other tech holdings.

body: Anthropic's second session was a reversal of its first. After a debut on Thursday that saw the stock open at $111.50 and close at $97.17, Friday's trade began about 9% lower at $88.17 and the shares spent the day in a range of roughly $83 to $92.56, ending at $88.91, down 8.5% (as of the 16:00 ET close).

The low of $83.05 left the stock five cents above its IPO price at one point. The share price has now fallen about 23% from Thursday's $115.10 intraday peak, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 5.0% and Nvidia 14% on Friday.

Also on Friday, Anthropic closed the offering. Underwriters took up the full 147m-share option, 15% of the 980m-share base deal, at $83, raising about $12.2bn more. Gross IPO proceeds rose to about $93.5bn, of which about $91.6bn goes to the company, and a concurrent $26bn private placement to partners including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC Partners took the total to about $119.5bn, before fees.

Research views remain split. Seaport Research sits at Neutral, describing the investment case as requiring a large leap of faith, while William Blair rates the stock Outperform. Earlier initiations included Needham (Buy, $150), Citizens JMP ($125) and New Street (Buy, $105), all of which are now well above the share price.
Supply is the next test: the first timed lock-up release is on 15 Dec, and up to 1.61bn shares can become eligible for sale by 2 Feb.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike in Talks to Buy Zscaler; Target Jumps 16% After Hours
stories.summary: CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler, Bloomberg and Reuters reported after the close on Friday 20 Nov, citing people familiar with the matter. Bloomberg put Zscaler's market value at about $32bn and CrowdStrike's at about $233bn, a combined $265bn. Both reports stressed that no deal is assured and the talks could end without an agreement; neither company commented. Zscaler shares rose 16.3% to $226.65 in after-hours trade (as of 19:59 ET), while CrowdStrike fell 4.8% to $218.34. A deal would add Zscaler's cloud network security to CrowdStrike's endpoint business, setting up a closer contest with Palo Alto Networks.
stories.market: ZS is down 13% this year, so a bid would rescue a laggard; CRWD's after-hours drop reflects acquirer dilution concerns. Palo Alto Networks (PANW), which rose 12.1% in the five sessions to 19 Nov, is the most direct listed rival.

body: Bloomberg first reported on Friday afternoon (about 13:05 PT) that CrowdStrike was in discussions to buy Zscaler, and Reuters followed, citing two people familiar with the matter. Neither report gave a price.
On Bloomberg's figures, Zscaler is worth about $32bn and CrowdStrike about $233bn, making a combination among the biggest in cybersecurity history. Reuters put Zscaler's value at about $33.5bn.

The strategic logic, per Reuters, is vendor consolidation: CrowdStrike's Falcon platform is focused on endpoints such as laptops and servers, while Zscaler sells cloud-based network security, one of CrowdStrike's main gaps against Palo Alto Networks.
Separately, Zscaler announced AI security work with Anthropic and Mistral at 16:05 ET on Friday. In after-hours trade ZS rose 16.3% to $226.65 and CRWD fell 4.8% to $218.34 (as of 19:59 ET).

Oracle shares rose as much as 3.3% in after-hours trade after the statement. stories.headline: Nvidia Plunges 14% on Record Volume as an SEC Accounting Probe Is Reported
stories.summary: Nvidia fell 14.01%, or $20.45, to $125.53 on Friday 20 Nov after Reuters reported that SEC enforcement staff are examining the company's accounting practices; Reuters noted that probes are not evidence of wrongdoing. Volume reached about 633m shares, roughly four times the 161m daily average, and the stock traded between $124.50, a new 52-week low, and $143.73. About $491bn of market value was erased in one session, and the shares are down nearly 50% from their October high of $243.37, and they lost 22.9% over the week. The fall came just three days after results showing revenue up 103% to $115.8bn. Fairlead Strategies' Katie Stockton called short-term sentiment contrarian bullish but said the long-term uptrend is broken.
stories.market: NVDA's drop led a chip rout: Micron fell 13.9%, AMD 13.3%, Broadcom 12.2% and TSMC 9.5%, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index lost 10.7% on the week. Nvidia rebounded 3.27% in after-hours trade by 18:02 ET.

body: Nvidia's slide deepened on Friday after Reuters reported that the SEC's enforcement staff is examining the chipmaker's accounting. The report added to pressure from a California investigative subpoena served on Thursday and from Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive on 12 Nov.

The stock closed at $125.53, down 14.01%, after an intraday low of $124.50. Trading volume of about 633m shares was nearly four times the daily average of 161m, and the stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since Huang stepped down.

Analyst targets have been falling for two weeks: Wells Fargo cut to $250 on 18 Nov and Freedom Broker to $230 on 19 Nov, both keeping positive ratings. Those targets now sit roughly 80%-100% above the share price, a gap that reflects how quickly the stock has fallen rather than any upgrade.

Technical strategists are more cautious. Fairlead's Katie Stockton said sentiment is stretched enough to support short-term rebounds, but described relief rallies as selling opportunities within a broken long-term trend.

analysts.view: Technical: short-term oversold, long-term uptrend broken

stories.summary: Taiwan's Taiex fell 2,393.60 points, or 6.23%, to 36,033.29 on 20 Nov, the third-largest one-day point drop on record, leaving it down about 17.5% for the week, its worst since 1991. body: The Taiex opened at 37,646.13 on Friday, sank to an intraday low of 35,738.68 and closed at 36,033.29, down 6.23% from Thursday's 38,426.89. It was the third-largest one-day point fall in the index's history and capped a week in which it lost roughly 17.5%.

The week began with a 2,635-point (6.03%) slide on 16 Nov to 41,040.08, when foreign institutions sold a net NT$70.19bn of main-board shares. On 19 Nov the index dropped another 1,768 points (4.4%) and fell below 40,000, with foreigners net sellers of NT$24.31bn.

Before Friday's open the Financial Supervisory Commission added three curbs to five measures it had announced on 9 Nov: a ban on short selling below the previous close for stocks that fell 3.5% or more the prior session, a narrower definition of short sales, and a cut in the daily cap on intraday short sales of borrowed shares to 1% of average volume from 3%. The Taiwan Stock Exchange pledged to keep markets orderly.

Investors cited doubts over AI valuations and profitability, rising AI-related debt, tighter US export controls on advanced chips to China, and uncertainty around Nvidia. Because TSMC accounts for more than 40% of the market's value, its 4.76% fall to NT$2,000 alone drove a large share of the drop.

analysts.view: Matthew Unterman said limiting short selling does not remove underlying bearish sentiment.
Charu Chanana said investors still back AI's potential but are questioning what to pay for it.

stories.headline: Kospi Closes 5.2% Lower at a 10-Month Low as Circuit Breakers Trip
stories.summary: The Kospi fell 267.93 points, or 5.21%, to 4,869.96 on 20 Nov, its lowest close since 20 Jan, and the Kosdaq lost 5.71% to 645.68; sell-side circuit breakers were triggered on both boards. Samsung Electronics slid 7.01% to 183,100 won and SK Hynix 5.92% to 1,113,000 won.
stories.market: Foreign investors net sold about 1.1 trillion won of Kospi shares while retail investors bought about 1.59 trillion won; the won weakened 6.2 won to 1,336.2 per dollar at the 3:30 p.m. close.

timeline.text: Previous Kospi sell-side circuit breaker.

Kospi rebounds to close at 5,137.89.

analysts.view: Cut its Kospi target for the second time in less than a month (new level not given in source).

stories.headline: Nikkei Sinks 5.1% as SoftBank Tumbles; Core Inflation Edges Up to 2.2%
stories.summary: The Nikkei 225 fell 5.06% to 56,436.65 on 20 Nov, its lowest close since 13 April, for a weekly loss of 7.7%, while the Topix dropped 3.88% to 3,674.22. October core inflation, released the same morning, rose to 2.2% from 2.1%, just below the 2.3% forecast.
stories.market: AI-linked names led the fall: SoftBank Group -14.48%, Kioxia -11.66%, Advantest -10.32% and Tokyo Electron -7.06% (20 Nov); the dollar held near 159 yen, and the CPI data keep a December BOJ hike in view.

stories.headline: ASX 200 Loses 5.4% in a Week as Miners Slump 12%
stories.summary: The S&P/ASX 200 fell 137.8 points, or 1.58%, to 8,592.6 on 20 Nov, its fifth straight loss, leaving it down 489.6 points (5.39%) for the week. Materials dropped 12.32% over the week, led by gold miners as spot gold slid to about US$3,522 an ounce, and technology fell 4.70% on the day.
stories.market: Megaport fell 12.89% and Xero lost A$4.48 to A$74.87 (20 Nov); the Australian dollar was flat near 66.6 US cents, with a Reserve Bank hold on 9 Dec widely expected after five hikes this year.

analysts.view: Now expects the RBA's first rate cut in August 2027, earlier than its previous November 2027 call.

watch: RBA policy decision on 9 Dec

stories.headline: Jakarta Stocks Slip 0.9% as the Vice-Presidency Stays Vacant
stories.summary: The Jakarta Composite Index fell 0.92% to 5,146 on 20 Nov, two days after Bank Indonesia's surprise hike to 6%. The vice-presidency has been vacant since Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigned on 12 Nov; President Prabowo Subianto must name two candidates by 25 Nov, and the assembly vote has been moved to 9 Dec at his request.
stories.market: Political uncertainty adds to pressure on the rupiah, which closed at 18,232 per dollar on 18 Nov, and on Indonesian bonds as Fed-hike bets lift the dollar.

timeline.text: Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigns.

stories.headline: Colombo Stocks Log Their Worst Week Since May After the Surprise Hike
stories.summary: The CSE All Share index fell 0.8% to 21,369.72 on 20 Nov, the day the central bank raised its policy rate 25bp to 9%, ending a three-week winning streak with a 2.97% weekly loss, the worst since mid-May. Governor Nandalal Weerasinghe said inflation, 8.3% in October, could reach about 9% by month-end.
stories.market: Foreign investors were net sellers of Rs52.6m on 20 Nov; the reserve-ratio rise to 3% from 9 Dec is set to absorb about Rs150bn of liquidity, and the rupee is down 6.9% against the dollar so far in 2026.

timeline.text: Monetary board meets; rupee closes at about 332.75 per dollar.
Policy rate raised to 9% and SRR to 3%; ASPI falls 0.8%.
Higher reserve ratio takes effect.

stories.headline: Karachi Bucks the Asian Rout as KSE-100 Gains 610 Points
stories.summary: Pakistan's KSE-100 rose 610.38 points, or 0.35%, to 177,382.57 on 20 Nov, extending its recovery for a second day while most Asian markets plunged. Traded value rose to Rs22.6bn, though decliners outnumbered gainers 259 to 211.
stories.market: Market capitalisation reached Rs19.26 trillion (20 Nov); reserves near $26.8bn in the latest week give support to the rupee and Pakistani dollar bonds.
